solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Range of mushrooms about right to fill belly

indicators.note: 'about' can mean turned round, so the word it follows is read from its end back to its start

parts.note: ceps are edible boletus mushrooms, a crossword favourite

indicators.note: filling something means going inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: tum is a childish, informal word for the stomach
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A forager's range of mushrooms, just right to fill a hungry belly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ceps are a favourite crossword mushroom, the porcini of Italian cooking; 'belly' here is the nursery word, not the anatomical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectrum is a full sweep or scale of possibilities, which is what a range is in the sense of variety.

clue.text: Architectural feature one associated with clubs in city

indicators.note: being in a place means being enclosed by it, so the small pieces go inside the larger one

parts.note: Porto is the Portuguese city (Oporto) famous for its wine
the Roman numeral for one
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Some grand feature of a city building linked with its gentlemen's clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests gentlemen's clubs or golf but is only the card suit, and the city is Portugal's second, home of port wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A portico is a roofed porch supported by columns at a building's entrance, a classic element of architecture.

clue.text: Church holding ancient stone, gold and silver in suspended state

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so the outer piece wraps around the rest

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
ancient means very old
st is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight (14 pounds)
or is gold in heraldry
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A church keeps its ancient stones, gold and silver treasures locked away, held in limbo.
explanation.walkthrough: CE opens and closes around a string of four abbreviations: C(OLD ST OR AG)E. A stone is a British unit of body weight, fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans put into cold storage are shelved, kept for later with nothing happening, so the phrase works as an idiom for suspension.

clue.text: Sometime Kent player, dealing with woman, tempted

parts.note: re means concerning or dealing with, as in business letters
Eve is the woman in Genesis who was tempted by the serpent

explanation.surface: A Kent cricketer caught up with a woman who led him astray.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent reads as the English county, whose cricket team has had many players; it is Clark Kent, and Christopher Reeve played him in the Superman films.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Reeve was the actor who played Clark Kent, Superman's alter ego, in the films of the late 1970s and 1980s.

clue.text: Locus for enthusiasts regularly using revolutionary toy

parts.note: a mecca is any place that devotees visit again and again

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the word next to it is read backwards

parts.note: to be on something (a drug, say) is to be using it

explanation.surface: A haunt where hobbyists regularly gather to play with some radical new toy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like an alternate-letters instruction but belongs to the description of the pilgrimage place. Meccano is the British metal construction kit with nuts and bolts.
explanation.definitionFit: Meccano is a construction kit of metal strips, bolts and nuts, a classic children's plaything first sold in Britain.

clue.text: Warehouse party held by university members

indicators.note: whatever is held by something is gripped inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: in 'town and gown', gown stands for the members of a university
a do is an informal party

explanation.surface: A warehouse rave hosted by students and dons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Town and gown' is the old British pairing of a university city's residents and its academics, so the members are the robe they wear.
explanation.definitionFit: Godown is the word used in India and East Asia for a storehouse at a port or factory.

clue.text: Fair to admit university mate manufactured overseas place

indicators.note: admitting someone lets them in, so the outer piece takes the others inside it

parts.note: a gala is a festive fair or fete
U is the abbreviation for university

indicators.note: something manufactured has been made up out of raw material, so the letters are remade into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A fair lets in a college friend with some foreign-made goods.
explanation.walkthrough: The container splits after its first letter rather than wrapping neatly around the middle, which is what makes this hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Guatemala is a country in Central America, which to a British setter is a land across the ocean.

clue.text: Act last from Art Pepper

parts.note: to do is to act

indicators.note: taking the last from a word means keeping only its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: The closing number from the jazz saxophonist Art Pepper.
explanation.walkthrough: Art Pepper reads as one name, the American jazz musician; the clue splits it, taking one letter from Art and using Pepper as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pepper a surface is to scatter small spots over it, which is to dot it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Closely-woven material taken to the cleaners

definitions.meaning: a fine, smooth woollen cloth made from tightly twisted yarn
slang for being thoroughly beaten or fleeced

explanation.surface: A tightly woven fabric sent off to be dry-cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs cloth with the dry cleaner's, but 'taken to the cleaners' is the idiom for being soundly defeated, which is to be bested.
explanation.definitionFit: Worsted is a smooth wool cloth, and as a verb form it means beaten or defeated, matching both idiom and fabric.

clue.text: Heavy sea wave meeting vessel — exciting ride?

parts.note: a roller is a long, heavy wave that rolls in
a coaster is a ship that trades along the coast

explanation.surface: A big wave slams into a boat, and that makes for a thrilling ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the ride is a fairground one, not a rough sea voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: A rollercoaster is a fairground attraction whose cars race up and plunge down steep tracks, the archetypal thrill.

clue.text: Time to publish a complex accumulation of lies?

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to issue a book or statement is to publish it

explanation.surface: Deciding it is time to go public with an elaborate web of falsehoods.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the phrase 'a tissue of lies', hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A tissue in the fixed phrase 'tissue of lies' is an interwoven web of untruths, so the idiom supplies the sense.

clue.text: Great price including first of beers: make it bitter?

parts.note: ace is informal for great or excellent

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a rate is a price charged

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A pub-goer grumbles that a great price on beer has left a sour taste.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is also a British style of beer, which the surface plays on; the question mark flags the rare verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To acerbate is to embitter or make sour, a rare verb related to acerbic and acerbity.

clue.text: Aggressive teller being awkward

indicators.note: awkward suggests clumsy and out of place, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A bank teller who is being difficult and turning hostile with customers.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder spans two words, 'teller being', with 'awkward' at the end as the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Belligerent describes someone hostile and eager to fight, a close synonym for combative or aggressive.

clue.text: Horologer struggling with a rabbit problem?

indicators.note: something struggling is twisting and writhing, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder; a horologer is a clockmaker
the letter itself

explanation.surface: A clockmaker fighting a plague of rabbits in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The rabbit is not the animal: in British slang to rabbit (on) is to talk endlessly, and the question mark signals that twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Logorrhoea is excessive, uncontrollable talkativeness, so a condition of someone who chatters on without stopping.

clue.text: Depraved sort soldiers will copy

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
probate is the legal proving of a will, and also the officially certified copy

explanation.surface: A corrupt type that the troops will imitate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' reads as a future-tense verb but is a noun, the testament, and 'will copy' together gives PROBATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled person of bad character, a noun for a wicked or morally corrupt individual.

clue.text: Cover over bathing beach

parts.note: a lid is a cover
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Putting a shelter over a beach used for swimming.
explanation.walkthrough: An over in cricket is a set of six balls bowled from one end; scorecards abbreviate it to O.
explanation.definitionFit: Lido originally named a fashionable seaside resort (from the Venice Lido) and now also means a public open-air pool.

clue.text: Meat cut seen around King's Lynn for instance

indicators.note: a cut shortens something, so the word loses its final letter
being around something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: VEAL with its last letter chopped off
R is Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A butcher's joint on display around the Norfolk town of King's Lynn.
explanation.walkthrough: King's Lynn is a town in Norfolk, but the clue splits it: 'King's' goes in the wordplay and Lynn becomes the singer Vera Lynn, the wartime 'Forces' Sweetheart'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vera is the given name of Dame Vera Lynn, so she is one example of a person called Lynn.

clue.text: Bean and cheese served with meat good to go

indicators.note: something told to go must leave, so that letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: Edam is the Dutch cheese with a red wax rind
GAME, the meat of wild animals and birds, without G for good

explanation.surface: A takeaway order: beans and cheese with some meat, all good to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good to go' reads as the takeaway phrase meaning ready, but G (good) is being told to leave the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Edamame are young green soya beans boiled in the pod, a Japanese snack, so the answer is a kind of legume.

clue.text: Pair periodically entertained by Darling Dicky?

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken into the house, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: precious is a term of endearment, like darling

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A couple now and then guests of someone called Darling Dicky, perhaps an old stage name.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a name, but in British informal speech dicky means shaky or unreliable, as in 'a dicky heart'.
explanation.definitionFit: Precarious means unstable and likely to give way, which is the meaning of the British slang adjective for weak or wobbly.

clue.text: Old money with capitalist's margins gone forever

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
tin is old British slang for cash

indicators.note: a word's margins are its edges, so only its first and last letters stay

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Old money and a capitalist's profit margins have vanished for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Margins' sounds like the capitalist's profits, but it means the edges of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extinct has died out completely, like a species with no living members, so it will never return.

clue.text: Girl with Don made out in the dark

parts.note: Una is a girl's name

indicators.note: something made out has been worked into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on and wear them

explanation.surface: A girl kissed a university don with the lights off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made out' reads as the American slang for kissing, and Don looks like a name or an Oxbridge tutor; it is the verb to put on clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To be kept in the dark about something is to know nothing of it, an idiom for being ignorant or uninformed.

clue.text: A match official in Wellington, or not in Wellington?

indicators.note: being in something means being enclosed by it, so the first pieces go inside

parts.note: a wellington is a rubber boot
a ref is a referee
the letter itself

explanation.surface: A referee at a match in Wellington, New Zealand, or perhaps not there at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellington looks like the New Zealand capital twice over; both times it is a wellington boot, the British rubber rain boot.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone going barefoot wears nothing on their feet, so they are certainly without any boot on.

clue.text: Club player in action endlessly before birdie

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: DEED, an action, minus its last letter
a jay is a bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A golfer in constant action before making a birdie.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf words throughout: club, player, birdie. The club is a nightclub and the birdie a plain bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A deejay plays records at a nightclub, so the answer is a spinner of music at a dance venue.

clue.text: Fabric from copper that insulates piping

definitions.note: a dhoti is strictly a garment, the cloth wrapped as a loincloth

indicators.note: insulating means wrapping around, so the outer piece surrounds the inner one

parts.note: a copper is a policeman, and DI is a Detective Inspector
piping hot means very hot

explanation.surface: Material made from copper for lagging hot-water pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper looks like the metal, and piping like plumbing; the copper is a police officer and piping is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A dhoti is a long cloth worn wrapped around the waist and legs by men in India, so it is a length of cloth.

clue.text: Foundation had a game plan slammed — there's nothing in it!

indicators.note: the phrase puts one thing inside the rest, so a piece goes within
something slammed is knocked about violently, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
O looks like zero, nothing
surface padding that frames the container instruction as a sentence

explanation.surface: A sports team's plan is torn apart by critics as having nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes in with the twelve letters of 'had a game plan' and all thirteen are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The first and last Greek letters stand for the whole of something, its essential basis and core principle.

clue.text: Metal mass Luigi Pirandello holds up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
a phrase that holds something carries it inside, so the letters sit across the words

parts.note: the letters straddle the two names

explanation.surface: The Italian playwright Luigi Pirandello holds up a lump of metal.
explanation.walkthrough: The playwright's full name is the hiding place; the letters run from the end of Luigi into Pirandello and are read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig is an oblong block of cast iron or other smelted metal, as in pig iron, straight from the furnace.

clue.text: Boatmen initially shoot two under Darwin's ship

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
in golf, an eagle is a score of two under par on a hole

explanation.surface: Sailors open fire at two targets below the deck of Darwin's vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' is the golfer's verb for a score, not firing a gun, so 'shoot two under' is a golf eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Beagle carried Charles Darwin on the voyage round the world that shaped his theory of evolution.

clue.text: Prime time with neither for broadcast?

definitions.note: a prime number, used as a noun

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters things widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Prime-time TV slot where neither programme is fit to air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime time' reads as peak viewing hours, but the phrase splits: Prime is the definition and time a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirteen has no divisors except one and itself, so it is a prime number in the mathematical sense.
